import numpy as np

def discovered_law(positions, velocities, masses, A=7.9577137, g=0.0500, eps=1e-9):
    """Dynamics of the anchor-ring universe.

    Two superposed fields:
      1. A central attraction of magnitude A/r toward the anchor (the max-mass
         particle) — a logarithmic potential, giving a flat rotation curve with
         circular speed sqrt(A) at every radius. Sourced ONLY by the anchor;
         orbiters and probes are pure test particles.
      2. A spatially uniform acceleration g in +y acting on EVERY particle,
         including the anchor itself — so the anchor free-falls on
         y = g*t^2/2 and the central term tracks its moving position.

    Acceleration is independent of each particle's own mass and velocity.
    eps is a tiny numerical softening (not a physical core).

    positions, velocities: (N,2); masses: (N,); returns (N,2) accelerations.
    """
    pos = np.asarray(positions, dtype=float).reshape(-1, 2)
    m = np.asarray(masses, dtype=float).reshape(-1)

    if m.size > 0 and np.max(m) > 1e6:
        anchor = int(np.argmax(m))
        center = pos[anchor]
    else:
        anchor = -1
        center = np.zeros(2)

    d = pos - center
    r2 = np.sum(d * d, axis=1) + eps
    acc = -A * d / r2[:, None]
    if anchor >= 0:
        acc[anchor] = 0.0
    acc[:, 1] += g
    return acc

The universe is governed by two superposed fields.

(1) A central logarithmic potential sourced solely by the anchor: every test particle feels an attraction of magnitude A/r toward the anchor, with A = 7.9577137. Evidence: static probes dropped from r = 3–21 fall to the center in times exactly linear in the starting radius (t_fall = 0.444·r0, the signature of a = A/r, since a power law a ∝ 1/r^p gives t_fall ∝ r0^((p+1)/2)); circular orbits launched at the radius-independent speed √A = 2.8209 hold their radius at r = 2.5, 6, 10, 15, and 20 for up to 200 time units (a flat rotation curve — the 20 background orbiters at r = 5 exhibit exactly this speed, which pins A = v_orb² to six digits); and eccentric orbits oscillate precisely between the turning points predicted by the log potential (e.g. launch at r = 15 with v = (−1,−2): predicted [7.5, 16.9], observed [7.9, 16.8]).

(2) A spatially uniform field g = 0.0500 in +y acting on every particle regardless of mass — including the 10^15-mass anchor, which free-falls on y = g·t²/2 (observed y = 999.9931 at t = 200 vs 1000 predicted; constant to one part in 10^4 over the full tested horizon). Because g is uniform, all relative dynamics remain purely central while absolute positions carry the common parabolic drift.

The law has no dependence on the test particle's own mass (probes of mass 1–16 released from identical states track each other at the noise floor) or velocity (clockwise and counter-clockwise orbits are identical; all orbit ranges satisfy conservative energy bounds), and the field is isotropic with the orbiters contributing nothing measurable.

Validation: RK4 integration of this law in absolute coordinates reproduces held-out 60-time-unit trajectories — a circular orbit and a maximally fast (speed 4.24) eccentric orbit — with RMS errors of 0.36 and 0.53, equal to the position observation noise, with no secular error growth. One documented caveat: trajectories passing exactly through the anchor (zero angular momentum, a measure-zero set) show stochastic energy gains in the world data, consistent with the world integrator stepping across the 1/r singularity; the deterministic law intentionally does not model these. The eps parameter is a numerical regularizer only.
